query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings, the dominant factor controlling wear is the in-situ formation and stabilization of a dynamic, ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous tribolayer during sliding. This nanolayer reduces the effective shear strength at the interface and acts as a protective barrier against wear.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy coatings initially exhibiting a coarse-grained microstructure with no pre-formed protective tribolayer.
generation.intervention: Apply in-situ tribological testing (using TEM or synchrotron-based imaging) under systematically varied normal loads to trigger and monitor the formation and evolution of the friction-induced tribolayer.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted during dry sliding tests in an inert or ultra-high vacuum (UHV) environment, under controlled normal loads, sliding speeds, and durations where oxidation is minimized.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous tribolayer at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: High local contact stress during sliding induces dynamic grain refinement and amorphization in the near-surface region. This morphological transformation creates a continuous, stable tribolayer that lowers the interfacial shear strength and mitigates material removal, thereby reducing friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: At moderate increases in normal load, the tribolayer will form more rapidly and uniformly, coinciding with a measurable decrease in friction coefficients (toward values around 0.2–0.3) and lower wear rates relative to the baseline low-load condition.
generation.baseline: Baseline wear performance characterized by tests at lower normal loads where any tribolayer formation is slower or less uniform, resulting in higher friction and wear rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under dry, low-oxidation conditions (e.g., in UHV) and moderate normal loads. At extreme loads or in oxidizing environments, other wear mechanisms (e.g., oxidative or adhesive wear) may become significant, potentially obscuring the effect of the tribolayer.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between normal load and the kinetics of tribolayer formation remains to be firmly established. Additionally, environmental variations (such as residual oxygen or temperature deviations) may also influence the nanolayer’s formation and performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ TEM or synchrotron-based tribo-testing on CoCrFeMnNi coatings while systematically varying the normal load. Monitor the real-time evolution of the near-surface microstructure and correlate it with simultaneous friction and wear measurements.
measurements: Real-time imaging of tribolayer thickness and grain structure changes via TEM/synchrotron
Recorded friction coefficients during sliding tests
Wear volume or wear track profiling post-test
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the normal load does not result in the earlier or more uniform formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous tribolayer, or if significant changes in tribolayer development do not correlate with expected reductions in friction coefficients and wear rates, then the hypothesis is refuted.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy-alloy (HEA) coatings used magnetron sputtering or laser cladding to deposit nanocrystalline films with improved wear behaviors. Researchers then explored how inverse Hall-Petch effects (ultrafine grains, dynamic amorphization) can reduce friction and wear rates. More recent works integrated reinforcements (e.g., TiC) or targeted specific CoCrFeNiTi compositions and refractory HEA films to increase hardness and lower friction even at elevated temperatures. Across these efforts, controlling microstructure, tailored defect structures, and tribofilm formation have proven key to enhancing wear resistance.
decision.unsolved: While individual studies highlight how fine-grain strengthening, phase transformation, or tribochemical layers can each improve wear, there is still no unifying mechanistic explanation that clearly identifies which near-surface transformation or structural evolution dominates for wear control across the broad range of HEA coatings and loading conditions.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ tribological testing (e.g., TEM or synchrotron-based) under controlled normal loads to track formation and stability of a friction-induced nanocrystalline/amorphous tribolayer in real time
decision.why: Recent evidence shows that wear performance in HEAs may be governed by the emergence of ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous tribofilms during sliding contact. Directly visualizing this layer as it develops could validate or refute the hypothesis that stable tribofilm formation is the primary mechanism controlling wear reduction. In-situ methods can capture the layer’s formation dynamics, crystallite size evolution, and correlation with friction and wear rates, providing clear mechanistic insight.
